newsitem.title: USA: Clinton won't rule out tobacco company immunity.
newsitem.headline: Clinton won't rule out tobacco company immunity.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Sunday left open the possibility that he could endorse a deal protecting tobacco companies from being sued by smokers whose health has been damaged.
Talks between top industry executives, states and a scattering of anti-tobacco forces began about two weeks ago concerning a settlement of suits by 22 states.

"I think we ought to see what kind of agreement they come up with and let me submit it to the public health experts and see what they say," Clinton said in an interview on CBS's "Face the Nation," taped on Saturday and broadcast on Sunday.

Clinton did not say which public health experts he had in mind, but late last week representatives of the American Cancer Society, American Heart Association, American Medical Association and American Lung Association expressed their strong opposition to granting the tobacco industry immunity.

Published reports have said the industry might pay as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers who fall sick with lung cancer and other diseases. In return, the industry would get broad shelter from lawsuits.

"On the limitation of liability, as I understand, what they've proposed to do is to create some sort of fund out of which people who are injured in the future could be compensated," the president said. "But they couldn't go through the tobacco companies."
Clinton's former chief of the Food and Drug Administration was skeptical last week about the possibility about reaching a deal.

"We simply can't negotiate away our children's future," said David Kessler on Thursday, adding he would oppose any settlement that did not grant the FDA authority to regulate the nicotine content of cigarettes and that did not require the industry to disclose its research on nicotine addiction.
On Friday, a federal judge in Greensboro, N.C., ruled the FDA can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes, but that it had no authority over advertising.
A leading anti-tobacco Democrat also opposes granting immunity to tobacco companies.
"We are opposed to any tobacco settlement in which we are forced to grant the tobacco companies immunity as the price for protecting the health of our children," Rep. Henry Waxman, D-Calif., said.
